profiles.meeting_scenario: At a 350-bed academic medical center, a hospitalist-led patient safety team and a nursing operations team are coordinating the rollout of a standardized bedside shift-to-shift handoff intervention on two adult medical-surgical units (4 West and 6 South). The meeting is a 30-minute coordination check-in one week before the pilot starts. The agenda is to align on what will be tracked during the first six weeks, how baseline and post-launch data will be assembled, and what each team will deliver to the shared dashboard. The expected outcome is a seemingly clear division of work: nursing will provide weekly handoff-related implementation data, and the physician lead will combine it with patient safety outcomes for leadership review.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.role: Hospitalist and Patient Safety QI Lead
members.expertise: Inpatient medicine, quality improvement evaluation, outcome measurement
members.background: A hospitalist with a master's degree in health services research who is leading a hospital-wide initiative to study whether standardized shift-to-shift handoffs are associated with fewer adverse events.
members.private_state: She wants a clean pre/post dataset that can survive scrutiny from executive leadership and potentially support a manuscript, and she is worried that messy operational definitions will make the intervention look ineffective.
hidden_assumptions: If the new handoff template is completed in the EHR, that is a valid operational marker of handoff compliance for the pilot dashboard.
The 'baseline month' should be the last full calendar month before staff training began, because training itself can already alter behavior.
Patients included in the pilot analysis are admitted adult medicine inpatients assigned to the two units; observation and boarding patients are outside the intended analytic cohort.
Safety events attributed to handoff effects are most meaningfully counted in the shift immediately following a handoff, not across a broader interval.

members.name: Maya Chen
members.role: Clinical Nurse Specialist for Medical-Surgical Operations
members.expertise: Nursing workflow design, bedside shift report implementation, unit-level auditing
members.background: A former charge nurse who now coordinates nursing practice changes across adult inpatient units and oversees bedside report training, unit audits, and nurse manager reporting.
members.private_state: She wants the rollout to feel workable for bedside nurses and is trying to avoid a measurement approach that depends too heavily on extra documentation or excludes patients nurses still experience as part of handoff work.
hidden_assumptions: Handoff compliance means nurses actually perform bedside SBAR with the patient and safety check; EHR completion alone does not show the handoff happened as intended.
The 'baseline' for nursing operations should be the most recent four weeks before go-live, because that reflects current staffing patterns and current reporting behavior.
Any patient physically present on the unit during shift change is part of the handoff population, including observation patients and overflow boarders, because nurses still hand off their care.
A handoff-related safety window runs until the next nurse-to-nurse report, because that is the interval for which the receiving nurse owns the consequences of the handoff.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about the weekly 'compliance rate' for the new handoff process.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Ortiz means the proportion of eligible handoffs with the new EHR handoff template completed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Maya means the proportion of handoffs in which nurses actually performed bedside shift report with SBAR and the bedside safety check, typically verified through audits or charge nurse attestation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In hospital improvement work, 'compliance rate' is a routine shared phrase, and both measures sound like reasonable proxies for the same intervention, so neither person feels a need to unpack the term in a brief coordination meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: Which dates make up the baseline
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to use the 'baseline month' or 'pre-launch baseline' in the dashboard.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Ortiz is thinking of April 1-30, the last full calendar month before handoff training started on the units.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Maya is thinking of April 15-May 12, the four weeks immediately before the May 13 go-live, because that is the period nursing leaders view as the most operationally comparable baseline.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both date windows are plausibly 'the month before launch,' and because each person assumes the relevant date logic is obvious from their own reporting practice, the phrase creates false consensus without triggering clarification.

misalignment_points.topic: Who is included in the unit handoff population
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'eligible patients on 4 West and 6 South' for weekly event tracking.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Ortiz means admitted adult medicine inpatients formally on those units and in the study cohort.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Maya means everyone nurses hand off on those units at shift change, including observation patients and temporary overflow boarders physically on the floor.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are discussing the same two units and the same handoff intervention, 'patients on the unit' sounds naturally aligned, even though one person is using an analytic cohort boundary and the other is using an operational workflow boundary.

turns.inner_thought: One week out, I need this locked down so the first dashboard isn't a patchwork of incomparable measures. If we can anchor the pilot on a clean pre/post structure, using EHR template completion as the operational signal and tightly defined outcomes, I can defend the analysis to leadership and maybe even build toward a manuscript.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. Since we're a week out from the May 13 pilot on 4 West and 6 South, I wanted to use this check-in to confirm the weekly dashboard inputs, make sure we're aligned on what gets sent over each Friday, and avoid any scrambling once the bedside handoff process starts.

turns.inner_thought: The rollout itself is in decent shape. My main concern is keeping measurement grounded in what bedside nurses can realistically do without turning this into one more documentation burden. Managers want something they recognize from unit practice, not an abstract analytic construct.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. From the nursing side, we're in good shape for go-live. The educators have finished the last of the in-services on both units, we've got coverage at both shift changes for the first few days, and the unit managers are on board and know they're expected to reinforce the process in real time.

turns.inner_thought: What I need is a weekly compliance rate based on the new EHR handoff template being completed for eligible handoffs. If the documentation rate gets to 85% by week two, that gives leadership a reassuring uptake curve and gives me something stable enough to pair with outcomes.
turns.utterance: Great. For the dashboard, one thing I'd really like to have front and center is the weekly compliance rate. If we can be somewhere around 85% by the second week, that will help leadership see early uptake rather than wondering whether the rollout is stalling.

turns.inner_thought: Eighty-five percent feels doable if we're talking about actual bedside SBAR with the patient plus the safety check. Charge nurses can do spot audits and managers can validate trends. I do not want this reduced to whether someone clicked through a screen in the chart.
turns.utterance: I think that's realistic. The charge nurses can help us capture the compliance rate during shift change, and we can use their spot checks to make sure the process is actually showing up consistently on the units early.

turns.inner_thought: I need the baseline month set before training contamination muddies things. For me that's April 1 through April 30, the last full calendar month before staff training started. If baseline creeps into the training period, the pre/post contrast gets softer and harder to defend.
turns.utterance: Perfect. The other piece I want to have in place from day one is the baseline month. I'd like to fold that pre-launch baseline into the same dashboard from the start so we're not building the comparison retrospectively after people have already seen the first few weeks.

turns.inner_thought: When he says pre-launch baseline, I assume he means the four weeks immediately before go-live, which is what nurse managers will expect to see because it reflects current staffing, census pressure, and present-day reporting habits. That's the fairest operational comparison.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I can pull the pre-launch baseline and make sure it's based on the most recent stretch before go-live, so the unit leaders are looking at numbers that reflect the current staffing pattern rather than something older that won't feel comparable.

turns.inner_thought: Now I need the unit-level events, but only for admitted adult medicine inpatients assigned to those two units. Observation and boarders are outside the study cohort and will muddy denominators. For handoff-related outcomes, I really care most about events in the shift immediately after the handoff, but I can sort that later if I have the weekly counts.
turns.utterance: The other data stream I'll need from your side is weekly counts for falls, medication errors, and code calls for eligible patients on 4 West and 6 South, so I can line those up with the handoff data and build out the shared view for the pilot period.

turns.inner_thought: That should be easy because our unit reports already cover everyone the nurses are actually handing off at shift change on those floors, including observation patients and overflow boarders. From an operations standpoint they're absolutely part of the handoff population, and the receiving nurse owns that interval until the next report.
turns.utterance: That should be straightforward. Our unit reports already cover everyone present at shift change on those floors, so I can package those weekly counts with the handoff information and send them over in the same file.

turns.inner_thought: Good. So by Friday she'll send weekly handoff data built around compliance from the EHR template, plus the baseline month and event counts for the study cohort. Once I merge that with the safety outcomes, the steering group should get a clean dashboard. This is coming together more cleanly than I feared.
turns.utterance: Excellent. So just to summarize what I have: you'll send the weekly handoff file along with the baseline numbers by Friday, and then I'll integrate that into the shared outcome dashboard so we have something ready for the steering group without a lot of last-minute rework.

turns.inner_thought: I'll frame this for the managers as a practical implementation tool. If the compliance rate stabilizes and the units can sustain the actual bedside process, they'll expect the dashboard to show whether the change is helping. I just need to keep staff from feeling this is about charting more rather than handing off better.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll remind the unit managers that once the compliance rate is steady, the dashboard should give us a pretty clean read on whether the new handoff process is helping, which will make it easier to keep people engaged through the first six weeks.
